claims.text: The multiphase eutectic HEA initially has a natural but imperfect passivating surface film.
The eutectic HEA contains chemically and structurally distinct phases capable of forming local micro-galvanic couples.
Al-Ni-rich regions act anodically while Cr-rich regions act cathodically.
Mechanical sliding wear erodes or disrupts the protective passivating film.
Wear-induced film disruption exposes micro-galvanic couples between adjacent phases.
Electrochemical-potential differences between exposed phases drive localized galvanic corrosion and selective anodic dissolution.
The exposed phase structure promotes localized differential aeration.
Elevated temperature near 700°C accelerates selective dissolution in this eutectic HEA.
Localized corrosion further undermines the integrity of the passivating film.
Galvanic corrosion facilitates more aggressive mechanical wear.
Mutual reinforcement between film removal, galvanic corrosion, and wear produces synergistically accelerated total degradation.
Producing a more homogeneous microstructure with fewer interphase boundaries minimizes micro-galvanic coupling.
The multiphase alloy will exhibit significantly greater total degradation than an intact-film or single-degradation-mode baseline.
Under identical coupled testing, the standard multiphase alloy will exhibit greater total degradation than the homogenized alloy.
The standard multiphase alloy will have greater wear depth and wear rate than the homogenized alloy.
The standard multiphase alloy will have higher corrosion current density than the homogenized alloy.
The controlled comparison holds temperature, normal load, sliding speed, and corrosive medium constant while varying microstructural homogeneity.
A lack of statistically significant degradation, wear, or corrosion differences between the variants would falsify the proposed mechanism as the primary cause.
